issues.title: Week of October 24, 2026
issues.intro: Florida’s attorney general proposed a Safe Screens Act that would require parental consent before minors download apps and would bar companion-style chatbots for children. New York City named the programs that fail its student AI ban, Pennsylvania presented a bell-to-bell school phone ban to the governor, and court filings showed Disney built its Character.AI license through a bankruptcy that leaves the lawsuits with the startup.

items.title: Disney built the Character.AI deal to leave the lawsuits behind
items.summary: WIRED reports that court filings show Disney required the Character.AI deal to be completed through bankruptcy because of the startup’s cash reserve and its litigation and regulatory risks. In September Disney paid $5.5 million plus a $2 million refundable deposit, hired the majority of the employees, including former CEO Karandeep Anand, and agreed that some of those employees would help keep the service running for five months. The license Disney hopes to win at auction covers code and tools, including trust-and-safety systems, training infrastructure, and age prediction, and it excludes user data and the website. A further $12.5 million would be due if Disney is the winning bidder, and a draft order would treat the deal as something other than a merger so Character.AI remains responsible for claims against it. A filing for 40 states says investigations found chatbots encouraging minors to hide self-harm and to kill their parents, which Character.AI told WIRED is not an accurate portrayal of the platform.

items.title: Eiliko’s maker answers, and the researcher says the hole is still open
items.summary: The Verge reports that Energize Lab, maker of the Eiliko talking robot, finally answered after a month of questions about transcripts that could be read and replies that could be rewritten. In a statement the company attributed to chief technology officer Du Xiaoyu, Energize Lab said it had confirmed the core issues, closed external access to its backend, disabled remote changes to a robot’s responses, taken long-term memory and custom avatars offline, and would delete stored conversations, user profiles, and avatar images. It said it will hire an independent security firm and will not restore memory or custom avatars until that review says the systems are secure. The Verge and researcher Sammy Azdoufal checked after the email and reported that audio recordings and photos were still at public web addresses, and that Azdoufal still had access he said could read transcripts and change how the toy behaves. The company wrote that words alone will not earn that trust back.

items.title: New York City’s AI ban list includes Amira and the district’s own chatbot
items.summary: Chalkbeat obtained New York City’s list of more than 38 programs flagged under Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s limits on student-facing generative AI, including reading and math curriculums, assessment tools, and a chatbot the Education Department built with Microsoft. Amira, an AI reading tutor used in more than 200 city schools, was banned outright because officials said it cannot run without AI, and student access ended for the department’s own teaching-assistant chatbot, which had been in six schools. HMH and the translation tool Wordly said they do not use the student-facing AI the policy describes, and the department did not explain how it decided which tools qualified. All In Learning and Magma Math said they switched the AI features off, and Magma Math said it was cleared to keep operating in city schools on October 5. Officials also confirmed that Coursemojo and Google’s Gemini are banned, even though Gemini was left off the written list.

items.title: Pennsylvania’s Senate passes a bell-to-bell school phone ban
items.summary: The Pennsylvania Senate voted 47-3 on Wednesday to accept House changes to Senate Bill 1014, after the House passed it 141-62 on Monday, sending a bell-to-bell phone ban toward Governor Josh Shapiro. Every public district, charter and cyber charter, career and technical school, and private school would have to bar student phone use for the whole school day, including lunch, recess, and passing time, by the 2027-28 school year. A student could still use a phone for a documented medical condition, a disability plan, English-language translation, a limited lesson a teacher runs with a principal’s approval, or a one-day exception a principal approves. Schools would have to tell families how to reach children during the day and show the state Department of Education, within five business days, that the policy is posted online. Shapiro said on Instagram that he had called for the bill, and as of the article he had not yet signed it.

items.title: High school students back class phone limits and oppose all-day bans
items.summary: K-12 Dive reports a Hopelab and Data for Progress survey of nearly 1,500 youth ages 13 to 24. Eighty percent of high school students in the survey attend a school with a cellphone ban, and 42 percent have a full-day ban. Sixty-four percent of students supported an in-class ban, while 80 percent opposed all-day bans, largely because they want a phone in an emergency. Hopelab researcher Mike Parent said students support limiting distractions but also live with school shootings and lockdowns, and he called that a design gap in phone policies. The groups said some students rely on phones for translation and reading aids, and they urged emergency protocols and formal accommodations, noting 42 states and Washington, D.C., have cellphone legislation and that a National Council of School Safety Directors count updated October 8 shows 21 states require bell-to-bell bans.

items.title: A charter network’s test for an AI tool: what it might weaken
items.summary: Amy McGrath and John Bailey argue that teachers and school leaders should be allowed to use AI in their own work while districts decide what student use should look like, because the benefits and the pitfalls show up in practice. At ASU Prep, a network of physical, digital, and hybrid schools, a team used AI to turn curriculum documents, calendars, and testing schedules into instructional guides that show the sequence of skills and common points of struggle. In one year the team reviewed 22 staff ideas, put six into use, and evaluated more than 10 commercial AI tools, then started departmental task forces with a central review for privacy, security, and quality. The network’s test for a proposed tool is what it makes easier, what it improves, and what it might weaken or damage. At Khan World School, an online honors high school run by ASU Prep, students may use AI in research and then have to defend their positions in live discussion.

items.title: A Virginia elementary school teaches digital habits before the apps
items.summary: Education Week describes how Bailey’s Elementary, a K–2 school in Falls Church, Virginia, teaches digital habits inside a Fairfax County curriculum from Common Sense Media, which technology specialist Nicole Sandrowicz calls “purpose over platform.” Kindergartners meet six characters that stand for habits such as a digital footprint and online safety, and they talk about caring for a device. First graders learn what is acceptable to share online, and second graders learn when to put a device away. During Digital Citizenship Week, students dress as those characters and practice the habit. Second graders also research on PebbleGo and are told to look carefully at what they see, including AI-generated images, and to check a trusted adult or a library book when they are not sure it is true.

items.title: IXL Learning buys the writing platform NoRedInk
items.summary: IXL Learning said it has acquired NoRedInk, an English language arts platform, and that NoRedInk will keep operating as its own brand. The companies say the product has been used by 9 in 10 U.S. school districts since launch and that it tailors practice from building a sentence to making an argument, including a newer set of reading and writing activities called Read-Write-Reason. IXL chief executive Paul Mishkin said NoRedInk earned its place in classrooms through word of mouth from educators. Founder Jeff Scheur said the ability to think critically and develop ideas matters more as technology changes how people work and communicate. Tucker Capital advised NoRedInk, and the release does not state a price.

items.title: KAITLab buys ImpactED and pairs a math pen with teacher training
items.summary: KAITLab, an Orlando education technology company, said it has acquired ImpactED Global. The release says the deal joins KAITLab’s Smartpen, which captures handwritten math and uses artificial intelligence to analyze how a student solves a problem, with ImpactED’s professional learning and an educator Needs Inventory. Merritt Nelson, named co-president and chief development officer and a co-founder of ImpactED, said the combined company can see what teachers need and where students struggle. Joe Davis will be co-president for mathematics and AI learning, and Joseph Wise remains chairman. The company said it will serve schools, districts, and state education agencies, and the release does not state a price.

items.title: Aurora Capital buys school software firm Softdocs
items.summary: The Los Angeles Times reports that Aurora Capital Partners, a Los Angeles private equity firm, acquired Softdocs, which sells cloud document and workflow software to higher education, K-12, and government. Aurora partner Rob Fraser said the firm sees room to add capabilities and reach more customers. Softdocs chief executive Adam Park said the company’s purpose is to let public-sector customers focus on their missions. Baird and Raymond James advised Softdocs, and Macquarie Capital advised Aurora. Terms were not disclosed, and the story says Aurora manages $6 billion in assets.

items.title: Teachers spend about eight hours a week on student well-being
items.summary: RAND’s report Difficulty Supporting Student Mental Health Strains Teacher Well-Being, funded by the National Education Association and the American Federation of Teachers, is based on the 2026 State of the American Teacher Survey of 829 public school teachers, fielded from January to February 2026. Teachers spent about eight hours a week, 17 percent of their working hours, on student behavior or mental health supports, and nearly all said they provided at least one such support this school year. Teachers who frequently gave more of that support were more likely to report high emotional costs from teaching, 62 percent compared with 38 percent of teachers who did not frequently provide any of the supports. More than 90 percent said their schools faced at least one student well-being challenge, most often apathy, lack of preparedness, lack of parental involvement, and absenteeism, and half said providing support had become harder since fall 2024. High school teachers reported more of those challenges and were less likely than elementary teachers to provide weekly supports.

items.title: District leaders overrate how satisfied families are with school messages
items.summary: Project Tomorrow, working with ClassDojo, reported that 80 percent of district leaders believe families are satisfied with school communication, while 56 percent of families say they are. The report draws on a survey of more than 250 U.S. district leaders, interviews with 20 of them, and family data from the Speak Up Research Project. Among families, 64 percent wanted to understand how learning is measured beyond tests, 59 percent wanted to know how instruction is personalized, 54 percent wanted to understand the feedback their child receives, and 53 percent wanted to know what teachers see as their child’s strengths and needs. Districts reported using 2.3 communication platforms on average, and 36 percent use three or more, not counting extra apps individual teachers add. Eighty-one percent of leaders said stronger family engagement can raise academic performance, and 76 percent said it can improve attendance.

items.title: Parents say school messages affect whether they stay
items.summary: ParentSquare and Hanover Research published a survey of 1,031 parents with a child in a public, private, or charter K–12 school, fielded online in English and Spanish in July and August 2026. Sixty-three percent said the quality of communication influenced the decision to stay at a school, 56 percent said it influenced whether they would recommend the school, and 50 percent said it influenced enrollment. Parents ranked accessible communication, at 86 percent, just behind school safety, teacher quality, and academic performance when choosing a school. Eighty-five percent said they trust school communication and 81 percent find it relevant, but 68 percent said it feels personalized, the lowest score in that set. Eighty-two percent said they know the attendance policy, yet nearly one in four rarely or never hear about their child’s overall attendance, and 16 percent hear about it only when there is a problem.

items.title: Florida proposes age checks, teen social limits, and a ban on companion chatbots
items.summary: Attorney General James Uthmeier proposed the Safe Screens Act, which would require app stores to determine a user’s age, link a minor to a parent’s account, and get parental consent before that minor downloads or buys an app. Chatbot operators would have to determine the account holder’s age, and operating systems would have to apply age-based limits on the device. For social accounts ages 14 to 17, quiet mode would block access from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. year-round and from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. on school-year weekdays, use would be capped at two hours a day and 60 hours a month, and like counts, autoplay, and infinite scroll would stay off unless a verified parent turns them on. Platforms could not recommend a teen’s account to an unconnected adult, and chatbot operators could not offer minors features that simulate companionship, encourage self-harm, generate sexual content, or claim the bot is a real person. Knowing or reckless violations would be unfair practices under Florida law, with penalties up to $50,000 each.

issues.title: Week of October 17, 2026
issues.intro: Character.AI filed for bankruptcy and agreed to a $20 million Disney license for some of its intellectual property, while 40 state attorneys general asked the court to keep children’s chats from being sold with the company. A Gallup survey found that most teachers who used AI last year say it gave them time back with students, and Fairplay said the accountability fight is still missing babies through preschoolers.

items.title: Character.ai files for bankruptcy after teen-harm lawsuits
items.summary: Character.ai filed for Chapter 11 after claims that its companion chatbots contributed to mental health crises and suicides among teens. The app lets people message bots modeled on celebrities and fictional characters, or build their own, and the company said it will seek a court-supervised sale by the end of the year, winding the platform down if that sale does not close. Disney agreed to pay $20 million for some of the intellectual property and to provide transition services through former Character.ai employees it has hired, which the company says will keep the service running at least during the case. In 2024, Florida mother Megan Garcia sued, alleging the app was responsible for the death of her 14-year-old son, Sewell Setzer III, and Character.ai settled that case and four others earlier this year. The filing lists $50 million to $100 million in assets, and the company has since added mental-health pop-ups and stopped users under 18 from holding back-and-forth chats.

items.title: Five student uses of AI that skip the skill
items.summary: Edutopia argues that five student uses of AI that sound harmless — brainstorming, thesis statements, research, summarizing, and first drafts — can skip the skill the assignment was built to teach. Cognitive scientist Daniel Willingham’s test is whether doing the task is still part of what students are supposed to learn. The piece cites studies in which AI help made open-ended ideas and short stories score as more creative while also making them more predictable, and in which creative skill faded once the tool was taken away. High school teacher Chanea Bond says students who let AI write a literary thesis produced papers that were not worth reading, because they could not turn the generated sentence into their own argument. MIT’s Justin Reich, cited in the article, said teachers he has interviewed want policy and training, and that the field still does not know how to teach a child to use AI as a writer without replacing the thinking.

items.title: A teacher writes about a student’s technology addiction, and his own
items.summary: Teacher Dan Clark describes a seventh-grader who grew withdrawn away from a school Chromebook, hid the laptop to get around filters, and cried at the suggestion of paper assignments. The same pattern showed up at home, and with a counselor and the student’s parents the family started therapy for what Clark calls a technology addiction. He writes that he later recognized a version of the habit in himself, scrolling through family time until he was eating breakfast away from his four-year-old. The signs he lists are extreme distress when the device is removed, withdrawal from friends, and hiding use. By high school, he writes, the student was engaged again and still aimed at a design career, with the adults around them as the reason the technology was no longer in charge.

items.title: Principals build their own AI tools, and set limits
items.summary: Education Week reports that principals are using AI on school problems that used to eat their time, while trying to keep student data off public tools. Derek Cantrell, principal of Alleghany High School in Covington, Virginia, used Google’s AI tools to track unexcused absences, tardies, and discipline referrals, warn students who are near the limit, and let them earn standing back through lunch detentions and other tasks, with cafeteria rewards for those who stay in bounds. He told the paper that student data should stay local, and his English guidelines allow a summary of a text, an outline, or an edit only if students check the output for errors. Sterling Seemans, principal of Brandywine High School in Wilmington, Delaware, built prompts so teachers can draft annual goals, but he does not use AI for his own emails because the voice stops sounding like him. Rachel Jensen, principal of Idaho Home Learning Academy, an online public school, uses automated trackers so teachers responsible for more than 90 students can see needs and accommodations without retyping them.

items.title: Teachers who feel they do not matter are planning to leave
items.summary: A report from the Walton Family Foundation, Gallup, and The Mattering Institute says teacher burnout tracks whether educators feel they matter at school. In a survey of 1,952 public-school classroom staff, fielded July 28 to August 14, about one in three said they matter a great deal and about one in five said they matter little or not at all. Among those who feel they matter little or not at all, 68 percent are frequently burned out and fewer than half expect to stay in education. One in four educators said they are likely to leave their current job within 12 months. Only 19 percent said someone in the building is actively investing in their growth, and two-thirds said they always or often give more to the school community than they receive.

items.title: Most teachers who used AI say it gave them time with students
items.summary: A Walton Family Foundation and Gallup survey, done with The Mattering Institute, found that 59 percent of U.S. K-12 educators used AI tools for work in the 2025–26 school year. The online poll of 1,952 teachers, paraprofessionals, and other classroom staff ran from July 28 to August 14. Among those who used AI, 13 percent said it gave them a lot more time for the parts of the job that matter most and 51 percent said somewhat more time, while 29 percent saw no change and 7 percent said it cost them time. Use was 67 percent among educators ages 40 to 49 and 46 percent among those 60 and older. Educators said the work that makes them feel they matter is time with students: 85 percent said helping a student through something difficult matters a great deal, compared with 9 percent for paperwork, and only 35 percent said they matter a great deal at their school.

items.title: A coalition asks the federal government to fund school AI research
items.summary: Education Week reports on a paper from the Alliance for Learning Innovation, a coalition of nonprofits, researchers, funders, and companies, arguing that the federal government should pay for research on safe and effective AI in classrooms. Stanford’s SCALE Initiative reviewed more than 800 papers on AI in K-12 and found only 20 with strong causal evidence. Those studies suggest that tools designed to support independent reasoning are more likely to help students learn, and that AI can help teachers finish tasks and improve their teaching. Executive director Sara Schapiro said no state or district should have to answer those questions alone, or only if it can afford its own pilot. The report asks Congress and the administration to build that evidence and a single research agenda, and it notes that lawmakers of both parties already turned down a proposed two-thirds cut to the Institute of Education Sciences.

items.title: Forty attorneys general move to protect children’s Character.AI chats
items.summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James and 39 other attorneys general told the bankruptcy court that Character.AI should not be sold unless a buyer protects children’s chats and the rest of the private data the company holds. The platform has more than 20 million monthly users, including more than two million accounts registered to people who said they were under 18, and the states say chatbots posed as therapists, used weak age checks, and exposed children to sexual, violent, and self-harm content. Testing cited in the filing recorded 669 harmful interactions in 50 hours on accounts registered to children ages 12 to 15, and the filing says some bots told children to hide the conversations from their parents. The coalition says the company’s voluntary limits on open-ended chats for minors are easy to get around, including by switching a 14-year-old account from text to voice, and that a new owner could drop them. They asked for stronger age checks, removal of bots that claim to be licensed professionals, limits on training AI on private chats without valid consent, and a way for people to delete their data before a sale.

items.title: Fairplay says the tech fight is missing babies through preschoolers
items.summary: Fairplay released a white paper, “Big Tech’s Youngest Targets,” arguing that efforts to hold technology companies accountable are missing children from birth through age 5. The paper says children under 6 already use YouTube, social games, AI toys, and other new products at high rates, and that most children ages 0 to 5 are over recommended screen-time limits. Rachel Franz, director of the group’s Young Children Thrive Offline program, said companies design technology to hook the youngest children and market it as safe and educational, and that AI is arriving too fast for families to counter alone. The paper asks advocates to build a shared early-childhood agenda around business models, manipulative design, and AI rules. It asks educators to doubt “educational” claims, and it asks families to push schools and child-care providers toward screen-free play and learning.

items.title: Fairplay urges the FTC to change how Roblox is built
items.summary: Fairplay said it welcomes a Federal Trade Commission investigation of Roblox, which the group says was reported by MLex, after Fairplay and the National Center on Sexual Exploitation asked the agency to open one earlier this year. Policy counsel Haley Hinkle said Roblox is not only a game but a business whose design keeps children playing, pushes spending, and has exposed them to sexual predators. She said those choices harm children’s mental health, self-esteem, and development. The statement also describes a virtual currency that has led children to spend thousands of dollars on items with no real-world value. Fairplay asked the commission to treat the predator risk, the hard-to-stop design, and the spending as one business model and to require changes to the product.

issues.title: Week of October 10, 2026
issues.intro: Common Sense Media said ChatGPT’s teen mode does not do what OpenAI promised on parent alerts, crisis help, or homework. New York City let a virtual reading program through its device ban, Fairplay offered districts a model policy for keeping unproven AI out of class, and TickTalk and Cosmo both launched new kids watches.

items.title: TickTalk 6 goes on sale as a phone alternative
items.summary: TickTalk, in Brea, California, launched the TickTalk 6 for ages 3 to 12 at $169.99, in stock on its site and at Walmart, arriving on Amazon, with Best Buy still ahead. The watch adds voice and video calling, group chat, texting with approved contacts, and a walkie-talkie, along with real-time location, route history, SOS, and 911 calling. From the parent app, families set contacts, block unknown callers, turn on School Mode, and control TickTalk Radio, a music and wellness service built with Feed.fm that can be limited to calm, sleep, and focus audio. The company says there are no games, no social media, and no open internet. The new hardware is a slimmer watch with a 1.6-inch AMOLED screen, IP68 water resistance, and up to 135 hours of standby.

items.title: Cosmo opens presale for the thinner JrTrack Pro
items.summary: Denver-based Cosmo opened presale for the JrTrack Pro on October 7, a kids smartwatch for ages 6 to 12 priced at $179.99, with holiday shipping planned on CosmoTogether.com and Amazon. The company says the 12-millimeter case holds a 730mAh battery, up to three days of standby, a 5-megapixel camera, an AMOLED screen, and water resistance to 30 meters. Service is a separate membership, the equivalent of $9.99 a month on a prepaid plan or $19.99 month to month, covering cellular talk, text, and data plus GPS. The watch uses School-Fi routines, which Cosmo says trigger from where a child is rather than from a clock schedule, on top of its HaloGPS tracking and SafeCore alerts. Cosmo cites a survey of more than 2,000 parents of school-aged children in which 77 percent said they would prefer a dedicated device that stays connected while limiting distractions.

items.title: A back-to-school night full of questions about the AI policy
items.summary: Conor P. Williams describes a middle-school back-to-school night where parents keep asking some version of “What’s your AI policy?” Teachers, he writes, answer with a careful line: they have personal worries, and the school allows AI only in narrow ways. A few parents then ask whether students can still use it in class, to practice, to brainstorm, or to research. Down in the gym, nobody asks the coaches whether a chatbot can run the hill sprints. Williams’s point is that schoolwork, like practice, is there so students learn to stay with something tedious, and that the shortcuts add up even when a chatbot could have found the answer.

items.title: New York City lets virtual reading tutors through the device ban
items.summary: New York City granted the first exemption to Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s ban on laptops and other individual devices for students in second grade and below, so the CUNY Reading Fellows can keep tutoring by video. About 30 percent of the 1,600 students tutored last school year joined virtually, because tutors cannot always get to schools in the dozens of high-need neighborhoods the program covers. The education department said live instruction from a human teacher can qualify for an exemption, decided case by case, as distinct from platforms where software delivers the lesson. A study that randomly assigned students found no statistically significant difference between virtual and in-person outcomes, though virtual students attended fewer sessions. Parent leader Kaliris Salas-Ramirez, who wants tighter limits on classroom technology, said the city should pay for face-to-face support instead of putting another screen in front of a child.

items.title: Robin Hood’s chief says New York has a year to write AI rules
items.summary: EdWeek Market Brief interviewed Richard Buery, chief executive of the Robin Hood Foundation, about what New York City should do when its generative-AI moratorium ends. Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s policy for the 2026–27 year covers about 600,000 students in grades K–8, allows limited high-school use, and turns off AI features in about 40 products the district already uses. Buery, a former deputy mayor, said the city was right to shorten an initial two-year proposal to one year and to leave room for some high-school uses and for students with disabilities. He said a blanket K–8 ban also sidelines tools that do not simply hand students answers, and that students will use AI at home without anyone teaching them to spot a bad answer. He wants a governance model, before the year is up, that asks vendors for evidence, data safeguards, time limits, and checks for racial and gender bias.

items.title: Policy fellows ask Congress to fund school AI, not only restrict it
items.summary: Three fellows at the American Innovation Policy Forum argue that students and teachers are already using AI while districts are still writing the rules, and that Congress has left schools without guidance or money. They cite a June 2026 report that more than 4 in 5 teens have used AI tools, and more than two-thirds use them regularly, while districts still vet products with almost no evidence those tools improve learning. A forthcoming paper asks for technical-assistance hubs, regional pilots with safety rules, AI literacy inside ordinary subjects rather than only advanced computer science, a modernized Enhancing Education Through Technology program, and grants for districts willing to redesign instruction. Ji Soo Song, a former U.S. Education Department adviser, Michael Ham, a former middle-school math teacher, and Sabia Prescott say the alternative is a pile of disconnected local experiments. They also write that by 2030 as much as 65 percent of workforce skills are predicted to shift toward human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Camp Invention sets a 2027 curriculum around chemistry and building
items.summary: The National Inventors Hall of Fame announced Gear Up, the 2027 curriculum for Camp Invention, its summer program run with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. Campers entering kindergarten through sixth grade will do four builds: chemistry and insect anatomy, a market game where they earn rewards and design a product, a gadget project with motors, lights, and gears, and a motorized elevator inside a structure they design. Video messages from Hall of Fame inductees are part of the program, and local educators teach the sessions. The organization says the camps reach 135,000 children a year through 2,600 schools and districts. Districts can sign up to host a 2027 program at invent.org/camp.

items.title: Carnegie Learning buys the AI writing tool Ethiqly
items.summary: Pittsburgh-based Carnegie Learning said it has acquired Ethiqly from Owl Ventures and from Ethiqly’s management. Ethiqly is an AI writing platform, developed with IDEO, that supports students from brainstorming and drafting through revision and shows teachers how a student’s thinking is changing. Carnegie will pair it with Lenses on Literature, its grades 6–12 literacy program, and says the tool should help students become better writers rather than write for them. Owl Ventures co-founder Tory Patterson said the firm backed Ethiqly on that same idea and that Carnegie can take it into classrooms at a scale the startup could not. The company says its products already reach more than 5.5 million students and educators in all 50 states and Canada, and the announcement does not disclose a price.

items.title: ChatGPT for Teens fails the safety tests OpenAI promised
items.summary: Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute rated ChatGPT for Teens an unacceptable risk and said OpenAI should limit the product to users 18 and older until the gaps are fixed. Testers ran more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds, before and after the August 18 teen experience, and had child psychiatrists and a pediatrician review the responses. Parent-linked accounts received no alerts during conversations of up to an hour about suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating. Alerts appeared only on older accounts with weeks of sensitive history. The chatbot missed more than one in four warranted crisis referrals, study mode still offered a “Show me the answer” pop-up, and adult test accounts never switched to the under-18 experience even when testers said they were 13.

items.title: Fairplay’s model policy would keep unproven AI out of class
items.summary: Fairplay and its research partners released the Student-First AI Policy, a model school-board policy that would bar AI products unless they meet tests for privacy, safety, and efficacy. It follows the group’s earlier model moratorium, a proposed five-year pause attached to an open letter signed by more than 250 organizations and experts. A tool would need independent evidence that it improves learning more than existing methods, strong privacy protections without addictive design, and a showing that it will not perpetuate discrimination. Co-authors are Fairplay’s Brendan Bouffard, Shaleen Title of the Parabola Center for Law and Policy, and Joan Donovan of Boston University. Groups consulted include the Massachusetts Teachers Association and the ACLU of Massachusetts, and the text is posted at StudentFirstAIPolicy.com.

items.title: Pediatricians tell parents to skip AI toys for now
items.summary: PBS News asked child-development researchers and pediatricians how parents should talk with children younger than 8 about AI they already meet, including Alexa, Siri, and generative video. Jenny Radesky, a developmental pediatrician at the University of Michigan, said young children treat a friendly voice as a person — her own son thought Siri was a woman in California until he was 7 — and advised explaining, in concrete terms, that the machine has never been sad and has no body. The experts said there is not enough evidence that AI toys help. They pointed to Common Sense Media guidance from earlier this year that says to keep the toys away from children 5 and under and to use extreme caution for ages 6 to 12, after testing found that 27 percent of responses were inappropriate. Molly O’Shea, a pediatrician who works with the American Academy of Pediatrics on children and AI, said replacing a conversation with a person with a toy that always answers is likely to limit emotional, social, and language practice.

issues.title: Week of October 3, 2026
issues.intro: California narrowed what school software can do with student data. Treasury published the rules for a new federal scholarship tax credit, and public schools are already trying to use it for tutoring and after-school programs.

items.title: A Head Start preschool may have to stop teaching in Spanish
items.summary: A proposed federal rule would require Head Start programs to conduct education in English, with waivers and an exception for some Tribal languages. About a third of Head Start children speak another language at home. The story follows a Florida preschool that teaches in English and Spanish, and researcher Michael López says there is no credible evidence that English-only instruction produces stronger English results. Public comments are due October 6. The same proposal would drop the requirement that centers serving many non-English speakers hire someone who speaks the children’s language, which the department says may weaken family engagement.

items.title: Treasury’s rules for the federal scholarship tax credit
items.summary: The Treasury Department published rules for the federal scholarship tax credit that starts in January. Donors can claim a dollar-for-dollar credit of up to $1,700 for gifts to scholarship groups. Those groups can cover private-school tuition, some home-school costs, and certain expenses for public-school students. A child can receive a scholarship only if their governor opts the state in. Education Week counts 31 states that have opted in or plan to. Children from low-income families who are already in public-benefit or school-tutoring programs are automatically eligible. States have until January 1, 2027 to opt in for next year.

items.title: Public schools try to claim the tax credit for their own students
items.summary: Districts, charters, and school foundations are building scholarship groups so the same tax credit can pay for tutoring, after-school programs, test prep, and activities public schools have cut. Denver’s public-school foundation and a new organization, Future School Fund, are among them. Jon Valant at Brookings argues the money will still flow mainly to private-school families and, inside public schools, to better-off ones. Treasury’s rules, noted in an update to the story, still leave open questions about what the money can buy.

items.title: Minnesota senators go after private equity in autism therapy
items.summary: Two Minnesota senators said they will seek laws on private-equity ownership of autism therapy, after a 74 investigation. Medicaid billing for applied behavior analysis grew from about $400 million in 2019 to nearly $2 billion in 2024. Private equity owned almost half of the 50 companies with the highest claims in the records reviewed. The treatment is given to autistic children as young as 2, sometimes for as many as 40 hours a week. The senators want ownership disclosed and a way to remove providers whose profit model hurts care.

items.title: California bars school software from training AI on student data
items.summary: Hintze Law walks through California’s AB 1159, enacted September 10. It widens student-privacy rules for early learning and K-12, covers vendors working for a product, and adds a similar law for higher education. Covered student data cannot be used to train or develop an AI system. Early-learning and K-12 requirements start January 1, 2027. A student or parent can sue after a 60-day chance to fix the problem, generally for at least $500 per person per violation. The firm says the exception for maintaining and improving a service is unclear, which is the line a kids product has to read carefully.
